item.title: Dad suffers heart attack days before daughter's wedding — then doctors make sure he walks her down the aisle
item.description: Rick Nelson had a heart attack days before his daughter's wedding, but after a quadruple bypass, his care team moved the ceremony to the hospital rooftop.
item.content:encoded:
A father who suffered a heart attack just days before his daughter's wedding refused to let open-heart surgery keep him from walking her down the aisle.

Days before the planned ceremony, Rick Nelson began having chest pains while at a friend’s home. His wife, Gail, rushed him to Cleveland Clinic’s Marymount Emergency Department, according to a hospital statement sent to Fox News Digital.

When it was confirmed that Nelson was having a heart attack, he was brought by helicopter to Cleveland Clinic's main campus. Doctors found multiple severe coronary blockages that would require open-heart surgery.

BRIDE IS WALKED DOWN WEDDING AISLE BY MAN WHO RECEIVED HER LATE FATHER'S HEART

As Nelson was prepped for surgery, he told his doctors, "My daughter, Rachel, is getting married Saturday. I have to be there."

Following a successful quadruple bypass performed by cardiothoracic surgeon Dr. Faisal Bakaeen, Nelson began recovering in the ICU.

The initial plan was for his daughter to come visit him the hospital so he could have a first look at her in her wedding dress — but that evolved into something much bigger.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Care teams from across the hospital worked together to make sure Nelson could take part in the June 6 wedding, coordinating every detail to safely move the ceremony to the hospital's rooftop.

Just days after undergoing life-saving heart surgery, Nelson traded his hospital bed for a front-row seat at his daughter's wedding. His care team prepared the venue, helped Nelson get dressed for the occasion and made sure he was able to walk his daughter down the aisle.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Nearly 80 family members and friends gathered on the hospital rooftop, where caregivers lined the aisle as Nelson — still recovering from the surgery he’d undergone just days earlier — accompanied his daughter to meet her groom, Dana Schultz.

"Moments like these remind us the work we do is about more than medicine. It’s about people, families and milestones that can’t be repeated — and the shared commitment of a team to make something so meaningful possible," said Dr. Bakaeen, according to Cleveland Clinic’s statement.

"It’s hard to put into words what this meant to us," Nelson’s wife said. "Everyone went above and beyond."

The celebration continued later that day at the couple’s reception, where the bride’s mother started her toast with a lighthearted quip: "He didn’t have to make this dramatic of a move to get out of giving a speech."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Nelson has since been discharged and is recovering at home with his family while beginning cardiac rehabilitation — grateful he was able to keep the promise he made to his daughter.

item.title: The war on data centers jeopardizes our economy and national security
item.description: Some 78 local jurisdictions have imposed data center bans or moratoriums, but the growing movement may only benefit China in the AI war race.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine if during World War II, protesters had gathered outside factories making tanks and planes, and tried to shut them down. Or that just before Pearl Harbor, when American industry was "hyperscaling" its defense infrastructure in order to make the country ready for war, cities and counties had placed restrictions on new plant and shipyard openings and tried to dictate what could be produced where — as long as it wasn’t near them.

Any commonsense observer in 1940-1941 would know the only beneficiaries of these obstructionist tactics were our nation’s enemies.

That was one kind of war. Today we face another kind, an artificial intelligence (AI) war with China. The aims of both combatants, in looking to dominate the technology that will rule the future, couldn’t be more different. While U.S. companies and the Trump administration see AI as a tool to make the world more prosperous and individuals freer and more autonomous, China’s goal in the AI sector is developing the tools to further enslave their own population while shaping a global hegemony "with Chinese characteristics," i.e. total control by Beijing.

BLANCHE URGED TO INVESTIGATE ALLEGED FOREIGN INFLUENCE IN FIGHT AGAINST DATA CENTERS

China and the U.S. are the only two countries poised to dominate the future of AI. Between them, they control 90% of AI compute capacity; yet America’s share comes to 75% compared to just 15% for China. It’s true China has focused on key applications in industrial use of AI, and also in treating AI as a decisive military and strategic asset. But the U.S. is still dominant in generative AI and AI innovation, and is moving fast to make up ground in the industrial and military spheres.

But not if the power needed to drive and expand our advantage economically and strategically, isn’t there.

How big is the data center ban movement? Some 78 local jurisdictions across the country have set up temporary moratoriums or bans on new data centers. While New York is the only state to actually impose a new construction moratorium, 14 other states are considering similar measures, including red states like Florida, Oklahoma, and Georgia.

MARXIST ORGANIZER LEADS CAMPAIGN AGAINST VIRGINIA AI DATA CENTER AS FOREIGN INFLUENCE CONCERNS MOUNT

If this movement grows and gets the backing of a major political party like the Democrats, and temporary bans become permanent, the only clear winner will be China, just as banning building defense plants in World War II would have benefited Nazi Germany and imperial Japan.

It’s not just the future of our economy that’s at stake: in Georgia’s case alone, some 552,000 jobs and $850 million in tax revenue if a ban goes into effect. It’s also our national security. I’d argue, even freedom itself.

Yet the ban movement itself is built on myths and lies.

TOP ENERGY GROUP WARNS WEALTHY FOREIGNERS ARE POTENTIALLY BANKROLLING ANTI-DATA CENTER CAMPAIGNS ACROSS US

Likewise, far from being a drain on the public fisc, tax revenues soar with the additional economic growth an AI-supporting data center helps to create.

Nor are the benefits just for billionaires and Big Tech. As a key driver of economic growth and productivity, AI will enable a host of startups and small businesses to compete in the marketplace, including the new recruits to a resurgent U.S. manufacturing sector.

By nearly every estimate, the onset of AI and its supporting data centers will add trillions of dollars to the U.S. economy — as much as an additional 1.5%-3.7% of GDP growth annually.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Those are the economic benefits. But AI, and the data centers that will enable its uses to grow and intensify, are also essential for our national security.

One side is AI’s obvious military uses, such as "killer drones" and other battlefield applications, as the war in Ukraine is demonstrating. But AI is also a powerful tool for detecting cyber threats, analyzing vast amounts of intelligence data and organizing the logistics for military readiness, not to mention making manufacturing in our defense industrial base more efficient and streamlined, and ready to take on China’s head-on.

Either way, the decisions we make now about the future of data centers will have a decisive impact on the future of freedom. It’s crucial that Americans choose the right path, one that truly benefits us and future generations; not the bureaucrats of the Chinese Communist Party.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM ARTHUR HERMAN

item.title: CNN staffers see Paramount merger as 'inevitable' despite legal battle delaying Ellison takeover
item.description: CNN staffers say morale remains grim despite a temporary restraining order delaying the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger that would give David Ellison control of the network.
item.content:encoded:
A delay in the looming Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery mega-merger that would put CNN under the control of David Ellison did little to quell anxieties at the struggling network. 

A CNN insider told Fox News Digital that everyone they’ve spoken to feels the merger is "inevitable" and said the delay hardly lifted spirits inside the company that has seen multiple leadership changes in recent memory. 

"No change in morale," the insider said. "Keep in mind the current situation is grim, so people see it as a matter of bad or worse." 

Ellison’s Paramount is attempting to build a media empire of historic proportions by acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery for $111 billion. The European Union and the U.S.’ Justice Department have each signed off on the deal, with the final roadblock coming from an antitrust lawsuit led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. 

Last week, a federal judge granted a temporary restraining order (TRO), temporarily blocking the companies from closing the deal until at least August 17. Paramount then agreed to delay the deal until next year in order for the lawsuit to play out in court.

PARAMOUNT-WBD MERGER ON HOLD AFTER JUDGE GRANTS TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDER

Some staffers are concerned about the direction of the network under Ellison, while others are worried about keeping their jobs. A second CNN insider, a longtime employee, is sick of the constant speculation. 

"I think most people just want whatever done, done," they told Fox News Digital. 

"I've been through multiple CEOs," they continued. "I've seen very little change based on who is at the very top."

There has been a revolving door of bosses who have run CNN in recent years. From 2013 to early 2022, then-CEO Jeff Zucker reshaped the network to be adversarial to President Donald Trump, particularly during his first term in office. After his ousting as a result of an undisclosed workplace romance he had with one of his deputies, Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav tapped Chris Licht, who worked as the top producer for MSNBC's "Morning Joe" and "CBS This Morning" before becoming the executive producer of "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert," to become Zucker's successor. 

PARAMOUNT ADVISERS PUSH FOR CALIFORNIA EXIT AS STATE SUES TO BLOCK WARNER BROS DISCOVERY MERGER: REPORT

Early in his tenure, Licht made clear he wanted to dial back the left-leaning programming that dominated the network during the Zucker era. However, he struggled to earn the trust of the CNN workforce, who were fiercely loyal to Zucker — an extremely hands-on leader in comparison to Licht — and were far more aligned with Zucker's vision for the network. 

Tensions came to a head in 2023 when Licht invited Trump on air for a CNN town hall, which sparked outrage among his staff and liberal viewers. Licht was publicly criticized by CNN personalities such as Christiane Amanpour and then-media reporter Oliver Darcy, while a somber Anderson Cooper told viewers he understood if they decided to ditch CNN forever. Employees got even more upset with Licht when an unflattering profile in The Atlantic revealed he told Trump to "have fun" prior to taking the stage. 

Zaslav ultimately fired Licht and replaced him with CNN's current CEO Mark Thompson, who has been credited for his effective stints leading The New York Times and the BBC. However, Thompson's own future at the network remains uncertain.

It was reported that Thompson insisted "he would not share oversight of CNN with another executive" after it was reported that Bari Weiss, Ellison's handpicked editor-in-chief of CBS News, would take on an oversight position at CNN after both networks are under one corporate roof. 

Thompson hasn't sparked internal strife the way Licht did, but sagging ratings, a confusing digital strategy and nonstop takeover rumors have caused continued dread within the company. 

"I think, for most, things haven't been the same since Jeff Zucker left," the second CNN insider said. 

WARNER BROS DISCOVERY SHAREHOLDERS APPROVE PARAMOUNT SKYDANCE DEAL

If Ellison does take control of CNN, the historic deal would come at least one year after his company acquired CBS News through a similar merger. 

Things haven’t exactly gone smoothly at CBS News under Ellison, as Weiss — like Licht — has struggled to earn the trust of her staff, infuriating liberals with changes seemingly designed to make the network’s coverage less partisan. 

Critics of Weiss and Ellison have accused them of bending the knee to Trump and trying to curry favor with his administration. CNN staffers now worry they will share a similar fate once Weiss and Ellison are handed the keys, though Ellison has publicly vowed that CNN will maintain its editorial independence.

The New York Times recently reported that "Ellison and his deputies are weighing whether to put Ms. Weiss in charge of CNN," adding that she could be teamed "with a more experienced TV executive who could handle the technical and financial aspects of the network." 

If Weiss is given control of CNN, it would mark an awkward reunion with Anderson Cooper, the veteran CNN anchor who served as a "60 Minutes" correspondent for CBS News until he walked away from the storied newsmagazine earlier this year.

Cooper has told colleagues that "he does not want to work" for Weiss, according to the Times. CNN contributor Kara Swisher has vowed to leave the company if Ellison takes over because his "handpicked minions" are "incompetent." 

CALIFORNIA AG BLASTS PARAMOUNT-WBD MERGER AS ‘ILLEGAL,’ SAYS THREAT TO LEAVE STATE IS ‘BLACKMAIL’ EFFORT

The Times also noted longtime executive Amy Entelis’ office has emerged as "something of a psychiatrist’s couch for anchors and correspondents, who often drop in to air their anxieties about the looming changes." 

CNN's star international correspondent Clarissa Ward passed on a long-term contract and opted to only extend her deal for one year in order to "evaluate the post-merger landscape and whether Weiss is given editorial oversight over CNN," according to Status.

The Status report noted that several of Ward's CNN colleagues have also expressed "strong reservations" about working for Weiss. 

If Paramount, which insists the state AG antitrust arguments are without merit, prevails, then Ellison could possibly enlist Weiss to finish what Licht was unable to complete. But it remains to be seen if CNN staffers will play ball this time around. 

CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP 

CNN declined comment when asked a series of questions, including if there is a concern that rank-and-file employees will turn on incoming leadership. 

Paramount issued the following statement: "This merger is lawful, pro-competitive, and will benefit consumers, creators, workers, and the entertainment industry. We will continue to vigorously defend the transaction and will look forward to the hearings on the substance of the State AGs’ action."

item.title: Caitlin Clark is missing from ESPN's new WNBA documentary and the filmmakers won't say why
item.description: ESPN's "Life in the W" follows A'ja Wilson, Napheesa Collier and DeWanna Bonner through the 2025 WNBA season but never explains Caitlin Clark's absence.
item.content:encoded:
ESPN released roughly two-and-a-half hours of a glossy documentary about the WNBA’s rise over the past few years. It's called "Life in the W," and it premiered Friday night, as part of an All-Star weekend rollout.

By Monday, someone could search the internet and find the trailer, ESPN press releases, streaming guides, episode listings and articles announcing the series. And that was pretty much it.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT TO PROTECT GIRLS AS WNBA ALL-STAR INITIATIVE BACKS ‘GENDER-EXPANSIVE’ GROUP

OutKick could not locate a single independent review of "Life in the W," a substantive interview with either of its key producers or even a traditional episode recap after the six-part series premiered.

That seemed quite unusual for an ESPN Original produced by UNINTERRUPTED in association with Cookie Jar & A Dream Studios, DICK’S Sporting Goods’ in-house content and production studio. None of those organizations is in the business of creating products and not marketing them extensively.

ESPN marketed the series as an intimate look at three of the WNBA’s "most accomplished and influential players" during a "groundbreaking year" for the league.

The lack of coverage is even more puzzling because the show’s publicity team actively pitched interviews with executive producer and show runner Trishtan Williams and ESPN Originals executive producer Lindsay Rovegno.

OutKick was offered an interview that never happened.

OutKick asked about interviewing the filmmakers on July 14. The following day, a publicist offered both Williams and Rovegno. OutKick immediately accepted, requested available interview windows and asked to screen the series beforehand.

Then, for more than a week, we heard nothing.

The publicist finally provided screener access on the eve of the premiere and apologized, explaining that the filmmakers’ schedules had become difficult because of WNBA All-Star events. Neither filmmaker was ever made available for the interview that had been offered.

Perhaps the rollout was simply disorganized.

But an interview with OutKick would have required the filmmakers to address the most obvious question hanging over the entire series.

Where is Caitlin Clark?

"Life in the W" follows A’ja Wilson, Napheesa Collier and DeWanna Bonner through the 2025 WNBA season. The cameras document their careers, families, relationships, injuries, playoff runs and participation in the negotiations over a new collective bargaining agreement.

Clark isn't completely absent. She appears in game and All-Star footage, and commentators mention her by name several times.

But she is not interviewed. She is not given a personal storyline. Her effect on the WNBA’s popularity is never meaningfully examined.

Instead, Clark exists mostly as background noise to a transformation the series repeatedly celebrates.

CAITLIN CLARK KEEPS DELIVERING RECORD WNBA VIEWERSHIP AS FEVER TOP 1 MILLION VIEWERS YET AGAIN

The opening montage touts the WNBA’s "recent surge in popularity," record attendance, increased viewership, new fans and a media-rights agreement worth billions of dollars.

Later, during a segment about Bonner’s brief and unhappy tenure with the Indiana Fever, the documentary describes a "new era in Indy" and an "influx of fans, viewership, marketing, money, all with the Indiana Fever."

The obvious catalyst for that influx goes largely unexamined.

It's difficult to make a serious documentary about the WNBA’s unprecedented rise without directly confronting Clark’s role in it.

It also may have been nearly impossible to include her.

That left the filmmakers with a clear Caitlin Clark problem.

"Life in the W" is missing its most important character

There are many potential reasons why Clark isn't one of the three players featured.

She may have been asked and declined. Given the level of scrutiny around her and how carefully her camp manages access, that wouldn't be surprising. Allowing cameras to follow her through an entire WNBA season would create considerable risk while offering her little she doesn't already have.

But the filmmakers would not say whether they asked Clark to participate at all.

There is also a practical storytelling problem.

The moment Clark becomes one of the central subjects, "Life in the W" becomes the Caitlin Clark documentary.

It wouldn't matter how evenly the filmmakers divided the screen time. Clark’s quotes would produce the headlines and her scenes would drive the conversation. Every moment takes on larger meaning when Clark is involved.

Wilson is one of the greatest players in league history. Collier is an MVP-caliber star and an important union leader. Bonner is a two-time champion and one of the longest-tenured players in the sport.

Put Clark next to them, and all three become minor supporting characters.

That might not be fair, but it is reality.

There's also the racial composition of the series.

Clark is the most conspicuous omission, but not the only one. Breanna Stewart, one of the most decorated active players in the sport and a WNBPA vice president, is not featured either. That makes the selection of Wilson, Collier and Bonner look less like a simple ranking of the league’s three biggest stars and more like a deliberate editorial construction.

Wilson, Collier and Bonner are all Black. Clark and Stewart are White. Paige Bueckers, the White guard selected No. 1 in the 2025 WNBA Draft, likely would have made a very interesting documentary subject, but she is also not featured.

That doesn't prove race was the reason for the selections, or even one of the reasons. But documentaries do not accidentally arrive at their central subjects. The filmmakers deliberately built the entire series around three Black women during an era in which nearly every conversation about Clark’s popularity, media attention and relationship with the rest of the league eventually becomes entangled with race.

The broader public debate surrounding Clark and the WNBA has repeatedly expanded beyond basketball into disputes about race, gender, sexuality, media coverage and who should receive credit for the league’s growth.

Adding the enormously popular White player would not have been a neutral casting decision; it would have changed the cultural meaning of the project.

The filmmakers could have faced backlash for making Clark the central explanation for a league that existed for nearly three decades before she arrived. Clark is the single biggest catalyst behind the WNBA’s recent surge in popularity, yet much of the league’s media ecosystem still appears reluctant to say that part out loud.

There's also the simple practical reason they may have chosen the players that they did: access. Being a central figure in a yearlong documentary process isn't for everyone. It requires allowing cameras and microphones to capture practically every moment in the subjects' lives.

It would have been perfectly defensible for the filmmakers to say they chose three women who were willing to grant extensive access to their lives.

They never gave us the opportunity to ask.

After the promised interview failed to materialize, OutKick submitted the central questions in writing: Was Clark approached? Did she decline? If she was not approached, why not? And what criteria were used to choose Wilson, Collier and Bonner?

Neither filmmaker responded.

Their lack of availability is especially strange in light of how little media attention the series generated.

The online coverage OutKick found consisted largely of announcement rewrites, ESPN’s own viewing guide, television listings and a favorable recap of a private promotional event hosted by Williams and attended by Bonner. None amounted to a substantive review or filmmaker interview about the series itself.

Even outlets that regularly champion women’s sports don't appear to have published a piece telling readers they watched the series and explaining why it mattered. Given the project’s focus on representation, motherhood, labor activism, LGBTQ relationships and three Black female athletes, one might have expected friendly coverage from progressive sports and culture outlets.

Instead, there was almost nothing.

WNBA COMMISSIONER VOWS TO CRACK DOWN ON 'RACISM, MISOGYNY,' DODGES BIG QUESTIONS AT ALL-STAR PRESS CONFERENCE

"Life in the W" tries to tell the story of a booming league through three accomplished women who had rich personal and professional journeys.

But Caitlin Clark still looms over the entire production.

CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP 

She is the unspoken explanation behind the "new era" in Indiana. She is the missing figure whenever the series celebrates the arrival of new fans, television viewers and money. Her absence also creates the documentary’s most interesting tension.

Clark is too popular to include without taking over.

She is too important to exclude without leaving a hole.

ESPN found a way to make nearly two-and-a-half hours of television with Clark mostly kept on the sideline. It never explained why.

And perhaps most remarkably, OutKick appears to be the only outlet that bothered to ask.

item.title: DNC Chair Ken Martin threw phone at aide's desk, faced HR complaint in sign of 'fraying nerves': report
item.description: A stressed-out DNC Chair Ken Martin allegedly threw his phone at a junior aide's desk, triggering an HR complaint as the DNC faces $18.5 million in debt before midterms.
item.content:encoded:
Stressed-out Democratic National Committee (DNC) Chairman Ken Martin faced a formal human resources complaint after allegedly throwing his phone at a junior aide's desk at the party's Washington headquarters in early July, The New York Times reported Sunday, as financial concerns and internal tensions placed his leadership under scrutiny.

The cause of the alleged outburst remained unclear, but one DNC source briefed on the episode described it as worsening conduct.

"It's just f---ing unacceptable. This is spiraling behavior," the source told NOTUS.

The Times described the show of frustration as a sign of Martin's "fraying nerves."

SLOTKIN SAYS DEMOCRATIC PARTY NEEDS 'NEW LEADERSHIP': 'OLD MODELS ARE NO LONGER WORKING'

The Times cited six people familiar with the incident, none of whom witnessed it firsthand. Their accounts differed over how forcefully Martin threw the phone, but the newspaper reported that it landed on the aide's desk while Martin was reprimanding the staffer and led to a formal HR complaint.

NOTUS reported that five sources said Martin threw the phone in the aide's direction after a scheduled period of donor and political calls. The phone did not strike the staffer, but several aides were shaken, according to the outlet. Martin apologized to the aide during an HR meeting on the following business day.

The reports came as the DNC faced a substantial financial disadvantage less than four months before the midterm elections. Federal Election Commission records showed the committee ended June with $16.3 million in cash and $18.5 million in debt. By comparison, the Republican National Committee reported $128.5 million in cash and no debt.

Martin is leading the Democratic Party in trying to win back control of the House and Senate in the midterms, in what is historically a buoyant year for the party out of power. Every president this century has seen their party lose the majority of at least one chamber in their midterms.

CASH-STRAPPED DNC SHELLED OUT MORE THAN $800K TO NON-VOTING TERRITORIES LIKE VIRGIN ISLANDS WHILE IN DEBT

According to The New York Times, he's resorted to joking about his job security and is "frustrated with the tarnished public image of a party that he plainly loves and has devoted his life to." He has also largely disappeared from public interviews in recent months following criticism of the party's bungled release of its 2024 "autopsy."

Fox News Digital reported in November that the DNC confirmed opening a $20 million line of credit and drawing $15 million. The committee pledged its partially owned Washington headquarters as collateral for the loan.

A DNC official said in a statement to The New York Post that the use of the building as collateral followed previous committee practices.

"This is not new. The loan documents were publicly released in November, and the DNC’s building was also used as collateral in our prior lines of credit in 2019, 2018, 2014, and many other years," the official said.

JAMES CARVILLE RAGES OVER FAILURE BY DNC TO RELEASE 2024 POLITICAL AUTOPSY, CALLS IT 'TOO STUPID FOR WORDS'

The Times reported that the committee asked some vendors to delay submitting invoices until after the midterms. 

In a statement to Fox News Digital, DNC Executive Director Roger Lau characterized those requests as routine contract discussions.

"This is nothing more than standard negotiations with vendors over contracts and payment processes," Lau said.

Martin defended the committee’s strategy in a Substack essay last week, saying it raised $154.8 million from grassroots and major donors through June, compared with $95.2 million during the comparable 2017-2018 period.

"The current DNC has raised the most money of any DNC without the White House in the 198-year history of the Democratic Party," Martin said in a Monday Substack. "But a party is not a savings account. Its purpose is to build power."

While the DNC responded to financial questions, it did not respond to Fox News Digital's request regarding Martin's alleged conduct with the junior aide.

item.title: Rep Thomas Massie says the Iran war has 'significantly weakened' America 'all for Israel'
item.description: Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky declared in a post on X that the Iran war has "significantly weakened" the United States of America.
item.content:encoded:
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky argued Sunday that the war with Iran has "weakened" the United States.

"The U.S. has been significantly weakened by the war with Iran," the congressman wrote in a Sunday post on X.

"This administration depleted our missile defenses, drained our oil reserves, sacrificed our men & women, inflated the price of consumer goods, increased our debt, and neglected our domestic needs…" he continued, adding, "all for Israel."

Some parts of Massie’s criticism align with publicly reported effects of the conflict. The Energy Department authorized the release of 172 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, while news reports and congressional spending measures have pointed to heavy demand for U.S. missile-defense systems and billions of dollars in additional defense funding. His broader assertion that the United States has been "significantly weakened" is a political judgment.

HOUSE REPUBLICAN THOMAS MASSIE SUGGESTS OBAMACARE COULD NOW BE LABELED 'TRUMPCARE'

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House early on Monday morning to request a comment.

Massie, who has served in the U.S. House of Representatives for more than 13 years, lost the May Republican primary in Kentucky's 4th Congressional District to President Donald Trump-backed challenger, retired Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein.

MASSIE LASHES OUT WHEN PRESSED ON EX-GIRLFRIEND'S ALLEGATIONS OF AFFAIR WITH GOP FIREBRAND

In a Friday post on X, Massie accused Trump of shifting toward a neoconservative foreign policy, writing, "Why did he flip to neocon?"

Former National Counterterrorism Center Director Joe Kent, who quit earlier this year due to his opposition to the Iran war, has been calling for President Trump to withdraw U.S. forces from the region.

EX-COUNTERTERRORISM OFFICIAL JOE KENT CONTINUES CALLING FOR US MILITARY WITHDRAWAL FROM MIDDLE EAST

"The Israelis know they can’t fight this war without the U.S., so their goal is to get us on board with more strikes, ground troops, etc., in the hopes that American causalities will sway public opinion enough to escalate into a chaotic, drawn-out war," Kent wrote in part of a Sunday post on X. "Our only viable option is to leave now—President Trump should use this pause in fighting to get our troops out & use quiet economic diplomacy to reopen the SOH & BAM."

The Trump administration has defended the military campaign as necessary to destroy Iran’s missile capabilities, cripple its navy, sever its support for terrorist proxies and prevent it from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The White House has also credited what it called "decisive American strength" with producing an agreement intended to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Cracker Barrel comeback gains steam as loyal customer says return visit 'felt like coming home'
item.description: A loyal customer says visiting a Cracker Barrel Old Country Store location "felt like coming home" as the chain raises its profitability outlook for 2026.
item.content:encoded:
After months of backlash over a controversial rebranding that alienated many longtime customers, Cracker Barrel Old Country Store is betting its future on returning to its roots, selling off secondary assets, cutting debt and focusing entirely on the iconic country restaurant chain.

The Tennessee-based restaurant chain announced last week that it has completed two major strategic moves designed to strengthen its core business, while raising its profitability outlook for fiscal year 2026.

The company completed a sale-leaseback transaction involving 26 company-owned restaurant locations, generating about $77 million in proceeds that it plans to use to reduce debt. It also sold most of its Maple Street Biscuit Company business to Biscuit Belly and said it will close the remaining 16 Maple Street locations, allowing the company to focus more heavily on the Cracker Barrel brand.

CRACKER BARREL SELLS MAPLE STREET BISCUIT COMPANY, CLOSES 16 LOCATIONS

"Our sale-leaseback transaction will allow us to opportunistically reduce debt while monetizing a portion of our owned real estate at an attractive valuation," President and CEO Julie Masino said in a statement. "Divesting Maple Street sharpens our focus on the core Cracker Barrel brand and is expected to improve profitability."

The moves come after a challenging stretch for the country-themed chain.

Last summer, Cracker Barrel faced vocal backlash over updates to its logo and restaurant remodels, with longtime customers arguing the company was abandoning the nostalgic look that had defined the brand for decades.

The criticism coincided with weaker sales and backlash that prompted company leaders to restore the chain's signature "Old Timer" logo and interior.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Among the chain's most outspoken critics was Tennessee resident Rachel Love, who previously told Fox News Digital she was disappointed by the changes. After recently visiting a restored Cracker Barrel that had undergone a remodel, however, she said the experience left her optimistic about the brand's direction.

"Going back to Cracker Barrel felt like coming home," Love told Fox News Digital. "Seeing the building returned to its original look honestly brought tears to my eyes before I even walked inside."

Love said the familiar brown exterior, welcoming Old Country Store and her favorite meatloaf meal made it feel as though the company had rediscovered what longtime customers valued.

"What has impressed me the most is that this turnaround feels like more than just cosmetic changes," she said. "It feels like Cracker Barrel listened to the people who have supported the brand for generations."

Love added that she is "genuinely hopeful about where the company is headed."

Restaurant industry publication Nation's Restaurant News recently reported that Cracker Barrel's comeback "continues to gain steam," noting that the company believes it could exceed its financial outlook for the year despite restaurant sales remaining slightly below last year's levels.

Cracker Barrel now expects to meet or exceed the high end of its previously issued revenue guidance and surpass its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) forecast for the fiscal year.

item.title: Rule Japanica: America and Japan are building the alliance China fears
item.description: Japan hosts 60,000 U.S. service members, covers 75% of basing costs and is now co-producing AMRAAM and SM-3 weapons systems at massive scale.
item.content:encoded:
These days, nobody does it better than Japan — especially from an American alliance perspective. From standing up to Chinese and Russian aggression to securing reliable supply chains, Japan and America are working together better, and with more urgency to coordinate and cooperate, than any other alliance around the world. In fact, Japan has pushed all its chips into the middle of the table to make an enormous existential bet on America. It’s time to say out loud what policymakers already acknowledge behind closed doors: for the United States, Japan has become the new special relationship in the world’s most important region.

Americans will always have a unique fondness for the United Kingdom, where our history, values and the bond of shared bloodshed, alongside family ties, will keep us forever close. And our intelligence relationship, which has no parallel in the world, will continue to make our alliance enormously beneficial to both Washington and London. However, in terms of pure military and economic value, the UK alliance provides far less than Japan. Given London’s recent economic pandering to Beijing, it has also become a far less reliable ally across the Indo-Pacific.

Geography matters. Japan, sitting at the center of the first island chain, constrains China’s access to the Western Pacific and secures U.S. access to the world’s most dynamic markets. Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s public statements have long implied a desire to push America out of the Pacific. When it comes to the deterrence of Chinese aggression and defense of the First Island Chain that the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy sites as core priorities, Japan is irreplaceable and its naval forces long ago eclipsed those of the U.K., Australia, or Europe. Other than Taiwan, no one else in the world is scrambling jets on a constant basis in the face of Chinese air incursions — 366 times in the last year. And when it comes to Taiwan, another vital U.S. interest, given its geographic position and its centrality to the AI revolution, Japan is the most forward-leaning. While other countries shy away from openly engaging with Taiwan, Tokyo is working with Taipei in public, is collaborating with the United States to reinforce deterrence, and is the most supportive of protecting the status quo across the Strait.

THREE KEY REASONS WHY AMERICA CANNOT AFFORD TO LOSE TAIWAN TO COMMUNIST CHINA

Ensuring America has access to the Indo-Pacific matters, and without a strong U.S.-Japan alliance, this too would be more problematic. Japan hosts approximately 60,000 U.S. service members and contractors, as well as another roughly 35,000 civilians — the largest U.S. military presence outside America. Japan covers roughly 75% of those costs, an average payment of $1.5 billion per year from Tokyo under the current agreement, which is another large bet on America. Japan is also home to the only forward-deployed U.S. carrier strike group in the world, at Yokosuka Naval Base, providing formidable and constant deterrence near the Taiwan Strait.

And Japan continues to step up, heeding President Trump’s call for broader burden sharing. Japan’s military expenditure rose 9.7% to $62.2 billion in 2025. Under Prime Minister Takaichi’s leadership, Japanese defense spending reached 2% of GDP in 2026, two years ahead of schedule, receiving plaudits across Washington. Japan’s defense budget has set a new record for 12 consecutive years, and the current Defense Buildup Program allocates approximately $275 billion over five years through 2027. This is putting your money where your mouth is when it comes to an alliance.

Japan is also thinking strategically, making sure American allies have the weapons stocks they need by co-producing advanced U.S. weapons systems at scale. Together, we are expanding co-production plans for AIM-120 AMRAAMs and increasing production of SM-3 Block IIA interceptors in Japan by fourfold. This makes Japan a defense industrial partner, not just a consumer, adding to allied production capacity to make up for munitions shortfalls. Integrating 400 U.S. Tomahawk missiles into the Japanese navy alongside the 2025 deployment of the Typhon missile system to mainland Japan increases the Japan Self-Defense Force’s interoperability while introducing real counterstrike capabilities.

At the same time, Tokyo is undertaking the intelligence reforms needed to develop a world-class intelligence community, one that is capable of and should be a "Sixth Eye," a member of the currently Anglo-centric intelligence sharing club called the "Five Eyes" made up of the U.S., U.K., Australia, Canada, and New Zealand. It’s a historic change for a country concerned with privacy and mindful of the lessons of the past, but it’s needed thanks to Chinese and Russian influence operations and will further tighten the U.S.-Japan Alliance.

Japan’s efforts don’t stop at its shores either. Following the successful Trump-Takaichi Summit in March, the Alliance has shifted into overdrive on critical minerals, establishing price floors, exploring new mining ventures, and bringing our private sectors together. At the same time, the Takaichi government has continued policies that shore up relations with Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands, strategic arenas very much at play in the broader competition with China. In Europe, Japan has been a major donor to Ukraine as well, pledging $6 billion in 2026 alone and providing $8.7 billion in budget support since 2022. When it comes to Africa, Japan has pledged $30 billion since 2022, moving to business-oriented partnerships which place trade over aid, in line with Trump Administration policies.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

In recognition — or maybe fear — of our closeness, China has tried to squeeze Japan by repeatedly sailing into the Senkaku Islands and by restricting its access to critical minerals. Beijing has even detained Japanese businessmen in Beijing in blatant instances of hostage taking. The result has only been to harden Tokyo’s resolve and emphasize the urgency of acting in concert with America.

TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO PAY UP. NOW ALLIES MUST TURN PLEDGES INTO POWER

We are truly in a golden moment with Japan, where we stand shoulder to shoulder to protect our shared interests, our supply chains and defend our allies and partners across the globe from malign actors. In meeting after meeting, at levels high and low, it’s clear that Japanese and American officials see the world, both its opportunities and its threats, from the same clear-eyed perspective and agree on what to do about it.

Washington should acknowledge this by admitting Japan to the Five Eyes club when it’s ready, standing up multiple defense co-production facilities on Japanese soil, and working with Tokyo to develop critical minerals processing plants across the world with jointly-financed processing and offtake agreements.

If only every other relationship was this special.

item.title: America’s tipping culture has gone from rewarding service to fee insanity
item.description: Tipping has morphed from rewarding outstanding service into an obligation that resembles a socialist experiment, with tip screens and hidden fees.
item.content:encoded:
I love old-school tipping; that is, letting a service provider know that you appreciate their outstanding service, whatever the realm may be, with a generous gratuity. It’s a great way for individuals to reward service providers who work hard and to signal your personal appreciation of the effort they have put in to your interaction.

However, tipping has morphed from a signal of good work to something that resembles a socialist experiment or the dreaded school group project: everyone expects the same outcome, regardless of their effort or the service they deliver.

When you order a cup of coffee at a counter today, they often present a screen asking you to include a tip. If tipping were acting as a price signal, as it should, then we would not know what to tip at the time of ordering. The tip would be given to a specific individual at the end of the experience, after you received your coffee, so that you could properly evaluate the experience and service to see if a tip is warranted, and if so, how much you would want to give.

AUTOMATIC TIP OR SERVICE CHARGE? NEW STATE LAW REQUIRES RESTAURANTS TO TELL DINERS BEFORE THEY ORDER

Making tipping an obligation upfront takes away the agency and valuable price signaling of tipping. In fact, it may be pooled with other tips and split by the group instead of rewarding the person who provided the service.

Tips, it seems, are being added to anything and everything. While it makes sense to tip your bellman who helps you with your bags to your room at a hotel, it does not make sense to tip on your e-commerce purchase, something I have seen popping up online from various retailers.

Additionally, many service businesses are abusing tipping, as well as other "service fees" and charges, to obfuscate pricing. Instead of raising their prices, some businesses are adding dressed-up fees to their bills. Customers want transparency in pricing, not to have to guess what the bill might be after all the added charges and fees.

CRUISE TIPPING CHARGES ARE 'OUT OF CONTROL,' SAY PASSENGERS AS COMPANIES TOUT 'EXCEPTIONAL SERVICE'

Cruise ships are adding "crew appreciation" charges. Restaurants are adding "surcharges" for reasons like "offsetting rising costs." That’s something that has typically been handled by increasing prices on the menu, transparently. Adding fees to the end of the bill doesn’t create loyalty; it feels like a business is pulling a fast one on you. Moreover, nobody likes to feel like they have been nickeled and dimed by a business.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Many of these charges are touted as "optional," with the businesses noting that customers can ask to have them removed from their bills. That seems more like a humiliation ritual than a good business policy. A customer shouldn’t have to go out of their way not to be inundated by extra charges.

Now, of course, I do have sympathy for businesses and service workers. There are certainly some customers who do not tip appropriately, even when service is outstanding. If that’s the case and your employees aren’t making enough, a more sincere solution would be to raise your prices and pay employees higher wages, being straightforward and not appearing like you are taking advantage of customers, which is likely to affect tip amounts, too.

Tipping is a time-honored tradition, and we should hold it as such. That means treating service providers well and tipping generously for very good service, where it is customary. It also means pushing back on non-transparent pricing tricks and distorting traditional tipping customs that have morphed into fee insanity.

item.title: Russia pulled back from the Arctic, for now. NATO must act before those troops return
item.description: Satellite imagery reveals Russia pulling air-defense systems from Arctic positions while building massive new bases near Finland and Norway's borders.
item.content:encoded:
While serving as an infantry battalion and brigade operations officer in Alaska, I learned that the Arctic is among the most unforgiving battlefields on earth. Aircraft can deliver soldiers to remote areas, but they cannot improvise roads, fuel or supply units once the fighting begins. In extreme cold, poor preparation kills soldiers as surely as enemy fire.

That lesson returned as I studied recent satellite imagery from Russia's far north. Advanced air-defense systems are disappearing from established Arctic positions even as Russia pours concrete for barracks and depots closer to Finland and Norway.

The two trends look contradictory. They are not. Russian President Vladimir Putin is operating on two clocks: sustaining today’s war effort while building options for a confrontation on NATO's northern flank once the Ukraine conflict slows.

TWO ICEBREAKERS HEADED TO ALASKA AS US COMBATS RUSSIAN, CHINESE INFLUENCE IN ARCTIC

Start with what Moscow is giving up. Near the Rogachevo airfield on Novaya Zemlya, Russia's Arctic archipelago, most air-defense assets at a longstanding missile position have been removed. Farther south, roughly two dozen S-300 and S-400 systems have disappeared from sites around Severodvinsk, the White Sea city where Russia builds and repairs nuclear submarines. Some protection may remain, but the reduction at these two vital locations is unmistakable. Russia is not abandoning the Arctic. It is accepting greater risk there.

Katarzyna Zysk, a professor at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, says the removals reflect "a growing mismatch" between the targets Russia must protect and its available launchers, interceptors and trained personnel.

UKRAINE UNLEASHES MORE THAN 400 DRONES NEAR MOSCOW IN ONE OF WAR'S BIGGEST ATTACKS

Moscow apparently judges that NATO is unlikely to launch an imminent large-scale attack on Russia’s far north. That calculation allows the Kremlin to thin its Arctic defenses without incurring what it considers unacceptable risk. The empty positions show what Putin believes he can afford to expose today, and the reason traces straight back to Ukraine.

Kyiv has imposed a tax on Russia's air defenses. Its long-range drones have threatened airfields, refineries and other facilities, forcing Russia to protect an expanding target list with a finite number of launchers, missiles and crews. Air-defense batteries have appeared near the repeatedly targeted Saratov oil refinery and even in Moscow city parks.

'PURE HELL' IN MOSCOW AS UKRAINIAN DRONES STRIKE MAJOR REFINERY SUPPLYING CAPITAL'S FUEL MARKET

The exact destination of each system can't be confirmed, but the pattern is plain: Russia is shifting scarce defenses toward the cities, refineries and sites it now considers most vulnerable. Every target that demands new protection leaves something else exposed, and every interceptor fired at a Ukrainian drone must be replaced.

Russia’s problem is no longer merely stopping attacks. It is deciding which targets matter most, and selected Arctic sites keep losing that argument. Russia's predicament is also NATO's warning: fixed air-defense sites, fuel depots and airfields are acutely vulnerable to drones and saturation attacks.

That triage helps explain the empty positions at Rogachevo and Severodvinsk. It does not explain the construction farther west, along NATO's newly expanded northern frontier. Satellite-based reporting shows expanding Russian military facilities along the Finnish and Norwegian frontiers.

At Pechenga, near the Norwegian and Finnish borders, an expanded base could eventually hold as many as 17,000 troops, up from roughly 7,000. Construction at Kandalaksha includes new barracks, ammunition depots and a headquarters facility, with activity also rising around Petrozavodsk in Karelia. Finland's army commander, Lt. Gen. Pasi Välimäki, has warned that Russian forces near the Finnish border could eventually grow from roughly 20,000 to 80,000.

That does not mean 80,000 troops are assembled there today; Russia remains committed to Ukraine, and buildings aren't battalions. But infrastructure changes what becomes possible. Barracks, fuel depots and rail connections determine how fast formations can arrive and how long they can fight. Moscow may lack the troops to fill these installations now, but it is making certain that a shortage of prepared bases will not limit its choices later.

Skeptics will argue that a military bogged down in Ukraine lacks the strength to open another major conventional front. They are right about Russia’s current limitations — and wrong if they conclude those limitations make it harmless. Moscow does not need to occupy a continent to create a crisis. It could seek temporary local superiority near a port, airfield or reinforcement corridor, combining sabotage, drones, cyberattacks and limited military action to test whether NATO responds as one.

Together, the empty missile positions and the expanding frontier bases reveal Moscow's sequence: defend the regime and the war effort now, and preserve the ability to regenerate and redeploy formations once the war slows, freezes or ends on terms that let Moscow rebuild.

The new bases do not prove Putin has decided to attack Finland or Norway; they show Moscow wants the capability available. NATO has a window between Russia's northern construction and Moscow's ability to fill it with regenerated forces, and that window will not stay open indefinitely.

The alliance has begun to use that window. The accession of Finland and Sweden has already strengthened NATO’s northern posture. In February, NATO launched Arctic Sentry to integrate allied activity across the High North; in June, it established Forward Land Forces Finland, pairing a Swedish battlegroup in Boden with a multinational staff in Rovaniemi. But new organizations matter only if they produce deployable capability, and what NATO needs now is a clear division of labor.

Europe should provide the conventional mass required to defend its own territory: ground forces, counter-drone defenses, hardened ports and civil preparedness. The United States should keep providing what Europe cannot quickly replace: space-based intelligence, undersea surveillance, integrated air and missile defense and the nuclear deterrent underwriting the alliance.

That division of labor requires an orderly transition, not a politically driven pullback. Washington should preserve the bases, intelligence links and logistics nodes that make reinforcement possible even as European allies assume more of the conventional ground burden.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

In any northern conflict, logistics would shape the outcome before the first shots were fired. Deterrence in the High North rests not on summit declarations but on ports that remain open, rail lines that keep functioning, fuel that reaches the front and interceptors that can be replaced within the first week, not the first year.

The Arctic punishes every planning failure: soldiers cannot fight if their vehicles will not start, their fuel freezes or their aircraft cannot land. The side that can move, supply and replace forces across the High North holds the advantage before the first brigade ever crosses a border.

Empty missile positions do not mean Russia is retreating. Unfinished barracks do not mean war is imminent. Together, they show Moscow accepting vulnerability now to preserve military options later. NATO must use the interval before those options become deployable. The time to prepare the Arctic is before the troops arrive.

item.title: Judge limits BBC from relitigating Jan 6 in Trump lawsuit over misleading documentary edit
item.description: A federal judge ruled the BBC can probe how Trump's Jan. 6 speech was interpreted but relitigating the Capitol riot is not at issue in the $10 billion suit.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge last week drew a sharp line around President Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC, ruling the broadcaster can probe how Trump's Jan. 6, 2021, speech was understood by the public — but cannot relitigate the riot at the U.S. Capitol itself.

The ruling was handed down by U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett as the BBC faces continued scrutiny over a 2024 "Panorama" documentary about Trump’s speech on Jan. 6.

The documentary — titled "Trump: A Second Chance?" — was subsequently labeled as misleading by critics who noticed it omitted Trump’s call for supporters to protest peacefully at the Capitol. The documentary stitched together remarks Trump made nearly an hour apart during his address that made it appear as if he had told his supporters to "fight like hell" down at the Capitol — the comments were actually out of context — shortly before the Capitol riot that day. 

"All of the impressions that were received by President Trump’s statements on Jan 6 are at issue," Lett said at the hearing, according to reports. "The full relitigation of Jan. 6 is not at issue."

TRUMP, BBC AGREE ON MEDIATOR FOR $10 BILLION LAWSUIT OVER JAN 6 DOCUMENTARY EDITING CONTROVERSY

A source close to Trump's legal team, which has accused the BBC of a "fishing expedition," said the judge's decision on that specific item was significant.

"It's important because this case is about a very limited splicing that consisted of nine seconds of a more than 50-minute speech and, rather than focus just on that, the BBC is trying to distract the judge, ultimately the jurors in this case, from that very limited scenario, and what they're trying to do is expand the scope of this case to litigate January 6 simply to take the attention off of them for their own wrongful conduct," the source told Fox News Digital.

"And so when the judge made that determination that that's not going to happen, that eliminated the primary defense that the BBC was seeking to employ in this case, which was to create a distraction, to make this case into something that was just going to be unmanageable and unnecessary, which is, 'We're going to try the whole January 6 case here.' The BBC has no standing, legal standing or any basis to bring such a defense."

Trump filed a lawsuit against the BBC in December in a personal capacity for both defamation and for a violation of Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act for $5 billion apiece, seeking $10 billion total.

At Tuesday’s hearing, Trump’s lawyers argued in a Miami courtroom that the president’s intent and third-party interpretations of his remarks were irrelevant because the lawsuit only points to the exact words Trump used in his speech, according to Politico.

JUDGE DISMISSES TRUMP'S $10B DEFAMATION LAWSUIT AGAINST THE WALL STREET JOURNAL OVER EPSTEIN STORY

"What matters is what he said relative to what was broadcast that he said. That’s it. There’s nothing more that needs to be examined," Trump attorney Alejandro Brito reportedly said.

Brito cited the written apology penned by BBC Chairman Samir Shah to Trump last year, in which Shah admitted that the documentary "gave the mistaken impression that [Trump] had made a direct call for violent action."

"He acknowledged the falsity," Brito told the judge, according to the outlet.

However, Sasha Dudding, an attorney for the BBC, noted that Shah had deemed the misleading edit as unintentional, and argued that the intent behind Trump’s speech is fair game for the outlet’s attorneys to investigate, Politico reported.

Dudding pointed to Trump’s own denial within the lawsuit, in which he asserted that he was not responsible for his supporters carrying out the riot at the Capitol, according to Politico.

FROM THE HUNTER BIDEN LAPTOP TO KAMALA HARRIS EDITS: THE LONG HISTORY OF '60 MINUTES' CONTROVERSIES

Ultimately, Lett ruled that while the BBC can delve into the interpretation of Trump’s speech by his supporters, the trial will not re-examine the cause or legality of the actual riot.

The judge also determined that the BBC overstepped in some instances regarding requests to examine the findings of several investigations into Jan. 6, the outlet reported.

The issue surrounding the documentary’s editing integrity comes after a report from The Telegraph revealed excerpts from a whistleblower dossier compiled by Michael Prescott, a communications advisor hired by the BBC to review its editorial standards.

The whistleblower alleged the network’s documentary spliced two separate comments made by Trump nearly an hour apart on the day of the Capitol riot, which erroneously implied that the president was calling for violence from his supporters.

LEGAL ANALYST PREDICTS TRUMP COULD WIN 'CONSIDERABLE' DAMAGES FROM BBC DOCUMENTARY LAWSUIT

"We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And I'll be there with you. And we fight — we fight like hell," the documentary showed Trump saying, without noting that the statement had been edited.

In reality, Trump said, "We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And we're going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we're probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them, because you'll never take back our country with weakness. You have to show strength, and you have to be strong."

Trump called on his supporters 54 minutes later to "fight like hell" for election integrity.

The controversy ultimately led to the resignations of BBC CEO Deborah Turness and Director-General Tim Davie last year.

What drove the majority of media attention and headlines this week was Lett ordering Trump to hand over financial information as part of the suit, according to Politico.

"All of President Trump’s brand, properties and businesses are impugned or said to have been impugned. Reputational, economic damages, all of that is now at issue in this case," Lett reportedly said.

EX-BBC DIRECTOR GENERAL TELLS NETWORK THEY SHOULDN'T AGREE TO PAY TRUMP ANY MONEY

Lett reportedly based the ruling on Trump’s argument that his businesses were negatively impacted by the network’s coverage, thus presenting the opportunity for the BBC to delve into the financial records of over 400 companies controlled by a Trump family trust.

This was widely covered as a significant blow to Trump. Headlines included MS NOW's "BBC to access Trump’s financial records as his dubious lawsuit starts to backfire," The Daily Mail's "Trump suffers humiliating legal blow in $10 billion BBC lawsuit," and The Guardian's "Trump must divulge financial details about businesses in $10bn BBC lawsuit."

However, a source close to the Trump legal team says the judge's order is "far more limiting" than what's been reported, saying she still must enter an order specifying what she'd require as part of the discovery process.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"The judge made it abundantly clear that although she's going to require certain financial information to be disclosed relating to the trust and the companies that are operated by the trust, that's not as broad as the BBC would like," the source told Fox News Digital. "At the end of the day, the financial information that they're seeking with regard to the Trump Organization has nothing to do with this case … We simply are viewing this in a way that's going to be far more narrowed and tailored than what's being reported."

Trump's team is now arguing he's only seeking amends for damage to his reputation rather than to businesses under his umbrella.

"This case is not going to be about any damage caused to the Trump Organization. It's always been about the damage caused to President Trump," the source close to Trump's team said.

While Lett reportedly said she does not possess the power to drop the business damages allegations from the suit, Trump can appeal the decision to one of his own appointees, U.S. District Court Judge Roy Altman.

The BBC, meanwhile, has argued the case should be dismissed on the grounds that a Florida court has no jurisdiction over what the British broadcaster aired across the ocean.

Fox News Digital reached out to the BBC for comment but did not immediately receive a response. 

Fox News Digital’s Brian Flood contributed to this report.

item.title: Katy Perry blasts White House for using hit song 'Firework' she sold in $225M catalog deal
item.description: Katy Perry blasted the White House for using "Firework" in a TikTok video of military strikes without her permission after selling song in $225 million catalog deal.
item.content:encoded:
Katy Perry blasted the White House for using her hit 2010 song "Firework" in a TikTok video without her permission, years after the pop star sold the majority of her music catalog in a reported $225 million deal.

On Thursday, the White House TikTok account shared a video featuring black and white footage of recent military strikes on Iranian targets, timed to the "boom, boom, boom" lyric from "Firework."

"Iran has been warned," the caption read, along with a firework emoji.

POP STAR OLIVIA RODRIGO FELT 'ENRAGED' AFTER ICE USED HER HIT SONG, BRANDS AGENCY 'BARBARIC'

In an X, formerly Twitter, post that she shared on Saturday, the 41-year-old pop star condemned the inclusion of her song in the clip.

"I am deeply appalled and angry to see ‘Firework’ used on the @WhiteHouse TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes," Perry wrote. "I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it."

"I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments," she continued. "To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponized to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for."

"My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare," Perry concluded.

The White House's post comes as President Donald Trump's administration remains locked in a tense standoff with Iran following recent U.S. military strikes and ongoing diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation.

When reached for comment, the White House directed Fox News Digital to an X post by Deputy Assistant to the President and Deputy Communications Director Kaelan Dorr.

WHITE HOUSE FIRES BACK AFTER ROBERT DE NIRO, BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN TAKE TRUMP SWIPES AMID COLBERT'S FAREWELL WEEK

In a reply to Perry's post, Dorr shared a montage of clips from the music video for the singer's 2012 song "Part of Me" in which the 13-time Grammy Award nominee was seen joining the U.S. Marines and undergoing military training alongside other service members.

"This you?" Dorr wrote alongside the video.

In September 2023, Perry sold her music catalog rights covering her first five studio albums to Litmus Music, a subsidiary of The Carlyle Group, in a deal reportedly worth $225 million. The agreement included her interests in the master recording royalties and music publishing rights for "One of the Boys" (2008), "Teenage Dream" (2010), "PRISM" (2013), "Witness" (2017) and "Smile" (2020).

Released in 2010 as the third single from "Teenage Dream," "Firework" topped the Billboard Hot 100 for four weeks and became one of the biggest hits of her career. The song's success helped "Teenage Dream" tie Michael Jackson's "Bad" as the only albums in history to produce five number one singles.

Along with "Firework," the sale also encompassed many of Perry's other mega-hit singles, including "I Kissed A Girl," "Hot N' Cold," "Roar," "California Gurls" and "Dark Horse."

Perry is the latest artist to clash with the Trump administration over the use of their songs in official social media posts. Other musicians who have recently objected include Ariana Grande, Kesha, Sabrina Carpenter, Céline Dion, Bruce Springsteen and others.

In June, Grande slammed the Trump administration for using her song "Bye" in a TikTok video depicting Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests, writing in the comments section: "please do not ever use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense. f-- ice."

The White House later fired back at the "Wicked" star in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

"We’ll say this one last time: what’s actually barbaric, inhumane, and heinous are the criminal illegal aliens who have injured and murdered innocent American citizens," White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson said.

However, the song was later removed from the video.

In March, Kesha denounced the White House on social media after it used her 2010 hit "Blow" in a TikTok video showing a fighter jet launching a missile at a naval target, saying the administration was using her music to "incite violence and threaten war."

"Trying to make light of war is disgusting and inhumane," Kesha wrote on X.

The "Die Young" singer said she "absolutely" does not "approve of my music being used to promote violence of any kind."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Love always trumps hate. Please love yourself and each other in times like this. This show of blatant disregard for human life and, quite frankly, this attack on all of our nervous systems is the opposite of what I stand for," the post continued.

At the time, Dorr responded in an X post in which he wrote, "Kesha quotes are like Popeye's spinach to this team. Memes? They'll continue. Winning? Will also continue."

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung also spoke about the topic on X, writing, "All these 'singers' keep falling for this. This just gives us more attention and more view counts to our videos because people want to see what they're b----ing about. Thank you for your attention to this matter."

item.title: Three dead, 2-year-old boy among 5 others injured in Seattle Center mass shooting
item.description: Three people were killed and multiple others were wounded on Sunday in a mass shooting incident at the Seattle Center, according to police.
item.content:encoded:
A suspect was taken into custody and police were searching for a second suspect after three people were killed, and four others were wounded Sunday in a mass shooting at the Seattle Center, according to Mayor Katie Wilson and police.

Wilson called the shooting "an act of horrific violence."

"Impacted families are living through the worst moment of their lives, and an entire community is trying to understand how a gathering built around culture, connection, and joy ended in gunfire," Wilson said in a statement. "No one should have to weigh the risk of being shot before attending an event, gathering with friends, or experiencing their city."

Police and emergency crews began arriving at the center shortly after 6 p.m. The venue was hosting the Bite of Seattle food festival over the weekend.

MULTIPLE INJURED AFTER FLOATPLANE MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING, CATCHES FIRE OFF WASHINGTON COAST

"Please avoid the area," Seattle Police wrote on X.

Police said one suspect has been arrested and they are searching for another. Investigators believe the two were shooting at each other and there is no ongoing threat to the public.

The Seattle Fire Department said two people were pronounced dead at the scene after attempting life-saving procedures.

Three other victims, including a 2-year-old, were transported to a hospital in stable condition, while a fourth victim was taken to the hospital in serious condition, the fire department said, adding that a fifth victim with minor injuries declined to be transported by first responders.

But officials have since updated the death toll to three without specifying which was the latest victim.

Harborview Medical Center spokesperson Susan Gregg said the injuries to the four patients involved an arm, abdomen and legs.

"Our first responsibilities are supporting grieving families, caring for the injured, and providing clear and accurate information for the public," the mayor said.

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson said he was receiving briefings and State Patrol SWAT officers responded to the scene to assist Seattle Police. He also urged residents to avoid the area and follow law enforcement instructions.

"My prayers are with the families of the victims, and the responders as they work to keep people safe," the governor said on X.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Seattle Police Department for additional information.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she was "absolutely horrified" by the shooting.

"My heart goes out to the victims and their families, and all those impacted by this senseless violence."

"I am grateful to the officers and first responders who are at the scene and working to protect our community, as well as the frontline medical professionals who are treating survivors," she said on X. "Tonight, we grieve with our community in Seattle as well as those around the country affected by gun violence and mass shootings."

King County Executive Girmay Zahilay similarly said he was "horrified" by the violence.

"As someone who grew up in this community, I know what this event means to so many families, young people, and neighbors across our region," he said in a statement. "For years, the Bite has been one of Seattle's signature summer traditions. To see violence at a place that brings so many people together is heartbreaking and unacceptable."

Kayla Carris, 22, said she was sitting outside the Armory at the Bite of Seattle when people began to scream and run for cover inside the Seattle Center Armory.

SEATTLE FIRE CREWS RESPOND TO 3-ALARM INDUSTRIAL DISTRICT WAREHOUSE FIRE, ROOF PARTIALLY COLLAPSES

"Everyone was just throwing stuff and running," Carris told The Seattle Times. "Like everyone."

Todd Behrends, 59, said he heard what appeared to be several rounds of shots.

People began running and jumping over each other to escape, Behrends told the outlet. One woman fell, and someone stepped on her leg.

Behrends said he saw a woman on the ground and a man on a stretcher as he ran toward an exit.

Harborview Medical Center is on modified lockdown for the victims’ safety following the mass casualty incident, according to an email sent to staff, The Seattle Times reported.

The Seattle Center Monorail was also closed for the remainder of Sunday.

item.title: Newborn vanished after secret birth, parents allegedly claimed baby 'was a prank': cops
item.description: The Florida couple allegedly claimed their newborn was "a prank" after the baby vanished, but investigators developed evidence for manslaughter charges.
item.content:encoded:
A Florida couple accused of claiming their missing infant never existed has been arrested in North Carolina after a yearlong investigation into the child’s presumed death.

Leon Alejandro Jr., 21, and Samantha Feliz, 20, both of Hollywood, Florida, were arrested Wednesday in Rockingham, North Carolina, where investigators say they fled while Hollywood police investigated the disappearance of their infant.

The pair were taken into custody by investigators with the Richmond County Sheriff's Office and the U.S. Marshals Service and booked into the Richmond County Jail on fugitive of justice warrants. They are being held without bond pending extradition to Florida.

Hollywood police began investigating the case in early 2025 after learning Feliz allegedly gave birth sometime between Dec. 6, 2024, and Jan. 5, 2025, according to the Richmond County Sheriff's Office.

DNA FROM SODA BOTTLE ALLEGEDLY LINKS MASSACHUSETTS WOMAN TO 1985 MURDER OF 'BABY BOY DOE'

Authorities said the birth was concealed and happened somewhere other than a hospital.

Investigators said family members saw the couple with the baby during the child's first month of life. After that, authorities said, the infant was never seen again.

According to an arrest warrant obtained by WPLG, investigators believe the child, identified only by the initials A.F., was last photographed on Jan. 5, 2025. Detectives wrote that the infant appeared "visibly ill and malnourished" and showed "no signs of life" in what they described as the final known image. 

The warrant also alleges investigators searched multiple locations with cadaver dogs but were unable to locate the child's remains, according to the outlet.

MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING PARTNER ARRESTED IN MEXICO NEARLY TWO YEARS AFTER FLEEING WITH THEIR TWO CHILDREN

Authorities allege Alejandro and Feliz repeatedly denied the child existed, telling relatives the baby "was a prank" and later claiming the pregnancy had been a "hoax" intended to scam family members out of money, WPLG reported, citing the arrest warrant.

According to the outlet, investigators said photographs showed Feliz visibly pregnant, while text messages discussed the pregnancy and the baby. 

Detectives also reportedly recovered baby clothing, a positive pregnancy test and what appeared to be blood-stained towels from a storage unit tied to the couple. DNA testing later determined blood recovered from the baby clothing and towels belonged to a biological child of Alejandro and Feliz, according to the warrant.

Despite the lack of a birth certificate or medical records, investigators said they developed enough evidence to charge both suspects with aggravated manslaughter of a child, tampering with or fabricating physical evidence, failure to report a death to the medical examiner, providing false information concerning a missing child and making false reports to law enforcement.

Authorities allege the couple fled Florida and were living on property belonging to one of Alejandro's relatives in Richmond County when investigators located and arrested them July 22.

'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' FUGITIVE CAPTURED ON SAILBOAT OFF NJ COAST AFTER 20 YEARS ON THE RUN

Richmond County Sheriff Mark Gulledge praised the multi-agency effort that led to the arrests.

"This is a prime example of agencies nationwide collaborating to uphold justice," Gulledge said in a statement.

Authorities have not publicly released additional details about what investigators believe happened to the infant.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Richmond County Sheriff's Office for any additional updates on the investigation, but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Jalen Brunson's Knicks status on full display as he walks in venue with wife while Nets star checks guest list
item.description: A viral video captured Jalen Brunson walking past security while Michael Porter Jr. checked the guest list at a Justin Bieber World Cup afterparty.
item.content:encoded:
There are levels to everything, even when you are a professional athlete.

Just look at what happened when Jalen Brunson, an NBA champion with the New York Knicks, and Michael Porter Jr., who stars for the Brooklyn Nets on the other side of town, arrived at a venue in a video that has since gone viral.

Brunson, who was alongside his wife, Ali, happened to arrive at a World Cup after-party hosted by Justin Bieber in New York City at the same time as Michael Porter Jr., who was with his former Denver Nuggets teammate Peyton Watson.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Porter may make more than Brunson per season ($40.8 million per season compared to $37.7 million), but the latter has achieved the ultra-rare "King of New York" status.

That means Brunson and his wife don’t need to wait in a queue or make sure they’re on a guest list when arriving anywhere. Porter, on the other hand, had to do just that.

TRUMP HYPES JALEN BRUNSON AFTER KNICKS SECURE NBA CHAMPIONSHIP: 'A SUPERSTAR WAS BORN'

The video shows Porter and Watson, who are both champions in their own right after winning the NBA title in 2023 with the Nuggets, needing to check in at the front door of the venue.

Meanwhile, the Brunson couple walked right through the front door, as camera flashes lit up the area right away.

"Mr. Brunson, how are you?" the security guard at the front door said to the NBA Finals MVP.

In New York lore, playing for the Knicks carries a certain weight compared to being in Brooklyn with the Nets. For one, the Knicks are the more iconic franchise, playing in "The Mecca" that is Madison Square Garden. The history, the rabid fans, and of course, this particular group led by Brunson winning the first title in 53 years, has electrified the city more than the Nets have.

The Nets moved from New Jersey to Brooklyn in 2012, and though they’ve had some teams with solid NBA All-Stars since then, they are never expected to take over the percentage of Knicks fans across the five boroughs.

The Nets have been in rebuild mode for the past three seasons, including Porter Jr.’s first during the 2025-26 campaign with Brooklyn. While he enjoyed career highs in points (24.2 per game) and assists (3), the team went 20-62 to finish third-to-last in the Eastern Conference.

Porter Jr. and Watson didn’t have trouble getting in after checking with the guest list coordinator, but the comparison between the Knicks and Nets got its latest debate topic.
